NO-REHIRE CLAUSE RESTRICTION IN SETTLEMENT AGREEMENTS — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This No-Rehire Clause Restriction in Settlement Agreements — Information Sheet is prepared for use alongside a settlement agreement resolving an employment dispute between Jordan Lee and Acme, Inc., dated September 1, 2026. It describes what California Code of Civil Procedure section 1002.5 says about no-rehire provisions in agreements settling employment disputes — provisions that would prohibit, prevent, or otherwise restrict Jordan Lee from obtaining future employment with Acme, Inc. or its parent company, subsidiary, division, affiliate, or contractor. This information sheet is not itself a settlement agreement, and it does not itself determine whether any specific provision in any specific agreement between Jordan Lee and Acme, Inc. is void, valid, or enforceable.

NO-REHIRE PROVISIONS VOID IN EMPLOYMENT-DISPUTE SETTLEMENT AGREEMENTS
California law provides that an agreement settling an employment dispute may not contain a provision that prohibits, prevents, or otherwise restricts a settling party who is an “aggrieved person” from obtaining future employment with the employer against which that person filed a claim, or with any parent company, subsidiary, division, affiliate, or contractor of that employer. A provision in an agreement entered into on or after January 1, 2020, that violates this rule is void as a matter of law and against public policy.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "(a) An agreement to settle an employment dispute shall not contain a provision prohibiting, preventing, or otherwise restricting a settling party that is an aggrieved person from obtaining future employment with the employer against which the aggrieved person has filed a claim, or any parent company, subsidiary, division, affiliate, or contractor of the employer. A provision in an agreement entered into on or after January 1, 2020, that violates this section is void as a matter of law and against public policy."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1002.5(a) (Leginfo text), California Code of Civil Procedure, Agreements Settling Employment Disputes, no-rehire provision ban (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1002.5)
  Known gap: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1002.5 is a distinct statute from Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1001, which separately restricts non-disparagement and confidentiality provisions covering the factual information underlying certain harassment, discrimination, and retaliation claims (that statute is covered in this corpus's Non-Disparagement Agreement — Information Sheet document). Section 1002.5 addresses a narrower and different subject: whether a settling employee can be barred from future employment with the employer or its corporate family. The voiding rule applies only to a provision in an agreement “entered into on or after January 1, 2020” — the statute's own text ties the void-as-a-matter-of-law consequence to that date, which is verified from the statute's own text rather than assumed; this indicates the rule is prospective rather than retroactive, though the statute's text does not itself state what result follows for an otherwise-identical provision in an agreement entered into before that date. The statute does not further define “parent company,” “subsidiary,” “division,” “affiliate,” or “contractor” within this section. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's current rule on this point — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific person's situation. This document is informational only and does not itself resolve whether a specific no-rehire provision is void in a specific case.

WHO IS PROTECTED: DEFINITION OF “AGGRIEVED PERSON”
The no-rehire voiding rule protects only a settling party who qualifies as an “aggrieved person.” The statute defines that term as a person who, in good faith, has filed a claim against the person's employer in court, before an administrative agency, in an alternative dispute resolution forum, or through the employer's internal complaint process.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "“Aggrieved person” means a person who, in good faith, has filed a claim against the person’s employer in court, before an administrative agency, in an alternative dispute resolution forum, or through the employer’s internal complaint process."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1002.5(c)(1) (Leginfo text), California Code of Civil Procedure, Agreements Settling Employment Disputes, definition of “aggrieved person” (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1002.5)
  Known gap: This citation is to a subsection of the same statutory section as the other clauses in this document (Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1002.5) — it is treated as one source with them, not independent corroboration of each other or of it. Because the voiding rule by its terms applies only to an “aggrieved person,” the statute's own text indicates it protects a settling party who has filed a claim through one of the listed channels in good faith; the statute's text does not itself extend the voiding rule to a settling party who has not filed such a claim. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's current rule on this point — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific person's situation. This document is informational only.

EXCEPTIONS: ENDING CURRENT EMPLOYMENT AND A PRE-CLAIM GOOD-FAITH DETERMINATION
The voiding rule does not preclude an employer and an aggrieved person from agreeing to end a current employment relationship. Separately, it also does not preclude them from agreeing to prohibit or otherwise restrict the settling aggrieved person's future employment with the settling employer where the employer made and documented a good-faith determination, before the aggrieved person filed the claim, that the aggrieved person engaged in sexual harassment, sexual assault, or any criminal conduct.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "(1) Preclude the employer and aggrieved person from making an agreement to do either of the following: (A) End a current employment relationship. (B) Prohibit or otherwise restrict the settling aggrieved person from obtaining future employment with the settling employer, if the employer has made and documented a good faith determination, before the aggrieved person filed the claim that the aggrieved person engaged in sexual harassment, sexual assault, or any criminal conduct."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1002.5(b)(1) (Leginfo text), California Code of Civil Procedure, Agreements Settling Employment Disputes, end-of-employment and pre-claim good-faith determination exceptions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1002.5)
  Known gap: This citation is to a subsection of the same statutory section as the other clauses in this document (Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1002.5) — it is treated as one source with them, not independent corroboration. This exception, by the statute's own text, has three specific conditions: the good-faith determination must (i) be made and documented, (ii) occur before the aggrieved person filed the claim, and (iii) concern sexual harassment, sexual assault, or criminal conduct specifically — it is not a general “any legitimate reason” exception. A separate, broader exception for a “legitimate non-discriminatory or non-retaliatory reason” appears elsewhere in this same subdivision and is addressed in the next clause; the two exceptions have different scopes and different timing/documentation requirements and are not interchangeable, as verified by comparing the statute's own text for each. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's current rule on this point — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific person's situation. This document is informational only.

EXCEPTION: LEGITIMATE NON-DISCRIMINATORY OR NON-RETALIATORY REASON
Separately, the voiding rule does not require an employer to continue to employ or rehire a person if there is a legitimate non-discriminatory or non-retaliatory reason for terminating the employment relationship or refusing to rehire the person.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "(2) Require an employer to continue to employ or rehire a person if there is a legitimate non-discriminatory or non-retaliatory reason for terminating the employment relationship or refusing to rehire the person."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1002.5(b)(2) (Leginfo text), California Code of Civil Procedure, Agreements Settling Employment Disputes, legitimate-reason exception (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1002.5)
  Known gap: This citation is to a subsection of the same statutory section as the other clauses in this document (Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1002.5) — it is treated as one source with them, not independent corroboration. Unlike the sexual-harassment/sexual-assault/criminal-conduct exception in subdivision (b)(1)(B), the statute's text for this exception does not include an express “made and documented” or “before the aggrieved person filed the claim” requirement, and it is not limited to any particular category of misconduct — this is a difference drawn directly from comparing the statute's own text for the two exceptions, not an inference beyond it. The statute's text does not itself define what qualifies as a “legitimate non-discriminatory or non-retaliatory reason.” This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's current rule on this point — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific person's situation. This document is informational only.

STATUTORY DEFINITIONS AND LEGISLATIVE HISTORY
For purposes of the good-faith-determination exception, the statute defines “sexual assault” as conduct that would constitute a crime under specified Penal Code sections (243.3, 261, 262, 264.1, 286, 287, or 289), assault with the intent to commit any of those crimes, or an attempt to commit any of those crimes. It defines “sexual harassment” as having the same meaning given in Government Code section 12940(j). The chapter containing this section was added by legislation enacted in 2019, and the section was later amended, with the amendment effective January 1, 2021.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "“Sexual assault” means conduct that would constitute a crime under Section 243.3, 261, 262, 264.1, 286, 287, or 289 of the Penal Code, assault with the intent to commit any of those crimes, or an attempt to commit any of those crimes. “Sexual harassment” has the same meaning as in subdivision (j) of Section 12940 of the Government Code."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1002.5(c)(2)-(3) (Leginfo text), California Code of Civil Procedure, Agreements Settling Employment Disputes, definitions of sexual assault and sexual harassment (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1002.5)
  "( Chapter 3.6 added by Stats. 2019, Ch. 808, Sec. 1. )"
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1002.5, Chapter 3.6 history note (Leginfo text), California Code of Civil Procedure, Agreements Settling Employment Disputes, chapter enactment history (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1002.5)
  "(Amended by Stats. 2020, Ch. 73, Sec. 1. (AB 2143) Effective January 1, 2021.)"
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1002.5, section history note (Leginfo text), California Code of Civil Procedure, Agreements Settling Employment Disputes, section amendment history (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1002.5)
  Known gap: These citations are all to the same statutory section as the other clauses in this document (Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1002.5) and to that section's own official history note — they are treated as one source with the rest of this document, not independent corroboration of each other. The cross-referenced definitions in Penal Code §§ 243.3, 261, 262, 264.1, 286, 287, and 289, and in Government Code § 12940(j), were not separately fetched or independently verified in this research — only § 1002.5's own text, which names them, was fetched and confirmed. The “void as a matter of law” consequence in subdivision (a) is tied to an agreement “entered into on or after January 1, 2020,” matching the chapter's original 2020 effective date; the source page's official history note also shows a later amendment effective January 1, 2021, but the statute's own text does not indicate that amendment changed the January 1, 2020 operative date attached to the void-as-a-matter-of-law rule. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's current rule on this point — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific person's situation. This document is informational only.
